slides.title: Course Overview: Econometrics and Statistical Foundations
Simple Linear Regression

bullets.text: OLS estimates minimize the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − b₀ − b₁xᵢ)².
The slope estimate is given by b₁ = Cov(x, y) / Var(x) or via normal equations.
The slope tells us how much y changes on average when x goes up by one unit.

slides.notes: We begin with simple linear regression, where OLS minimizes squared residuals to find the best-fitting line. Remember that variance from your probability notes underlies these estimators.

slides.title: OLS Assumptions and Gauss-Markov Theorem

bullets.text: The first Gauss-Markov assumption is that the population process is linear in parameters.
MLR.5 defines homoskedasticity: Var(u | x₁, …, xₖ) = σ², meaning error variance does not depend on regressors.
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE: the best linear unbiased estimator.

slides.notes: Here we establish the famous Gauss-Markov theorem. Unbiasedness requires the first four assumptions, while homoskedasticity is required for OLS to be fully efficient as BLUE.

slides.title: Multiple Regression and OVB

bullets.text: β₁ measures the effect of x₁ on y holding x₂ fixed, providing a ceteris paribus interpretation.
Omitting a relevant variable that is correlated with x₁ introduces omitted variable bias into b₁.
The omitted variable bias equals Bias(b̃₁) = β₂ · δ̃₁, where δ̃₁ comes from regressing x₂ on x₁.

slides.notes: Multiple regression lets us control for other factors. Be very careful with omitted variables, as failing to include a relevant regressor biases your slope estimate.

slides.title: Hypothesis Testing: t and F

bullets.text: The t-test statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error, compared to a t distribution with n − 2 degrees of freedom.
The F-test evaluates multiple restrictions simultaneously, asking how much worse the fit gets if coefficients are forced to zero.

slides.notes: For hypothesis testing, we use t-tests for individual coefficients and F-tests to check joint restrictions using restricted and unrestricted models.

slides.title: Dummy Variables and Interactions

bullets.text: An interaction term allows the effect of one variable on the outcome to depend on the value of another variable.
To avoid the dummy variable trap, include g − 1 dummies for g groups when an intercept is present to prevent perfect collinearity.

slides.notes: Dummy variables capture qualitative factors. Always remember to drop one category to avoid the dummy variable trap.

slides.title: Autocorrelation in Time Series

bullets.text: Autocorrelation means that the error in the current period is correlated with the error in the previous period.
With AR(1) errors defined by uₜ = ρuₜ₋₁ + eₜ, OLS remains unbiased but standard errors become invalid.
The Durbin–Watson statistic d ≈ 2(1 − ρ̂) helps detect autocorrelation, with values near 2 indicating no first-order serial correlation.

slides.notes: When moving to time series, errors can be correlated over time. While OLS stays unbiased under AR(1) errors, standard errors are ruined, so we rely on checks like Durbin-Watson.

slides.title: Key Takeaways

bullets.text: OLS minimizes squared residuals, and its statistical properties rely heavily on the Gauss-Markov assumptions.
Omitted variables cause bias, while proper hypothesis testing uses t and F statistics to evaluate coefficient restrictions.
Time series models require caution regarding autocorrelation, connecting back to the variance and expectation concepts from probability.

slides.notes: To ace your exam, make sure you understand the core OLS mechanics, the Gauss-Markov conditions, and how omitted variables or autocorrelation disrupt standard inferences.
